barcelona.name: La Rambla
barcelona.summary: The tree-lined boulevard running 1.2 km from Plaça de Catalunya to the old harbour, past La Boqueria and the Liceu opera house.
barcelona.expect: Crowded and touristy, with pickpockets working the busiest stretch; most locals walk the side streets instead.
barcelona.tip: Walk it once early in the morning, then turn into the Gothic Quarter or El Raval rather than eating on the boulevard.
barcelona.why: It has been the city's main promenade since the 18th century and links the old town to the sea.
flow: Start at Plaça de Catalunya.
Stop at La Boqueria and the Miró mosaic in the pavement.
Finish at the Columbus Monument by the port.
barcelona.bestFor: A first walk through the old town

barcelona.name: Palau de la Música Catalana
barcelona.summary: A 1908 concert hall by Domènech i Montaner, with a stained-glass skylight and sculpted stage that make it the jewel of Catalan Modernisme.
barcelona.expect: Seen on a guided tour or, better, at a concert; tours run in several languages through the day.
barcelona.tip: Book a concert ticket instead of a tour: the hall is at its best full of sound and evening light.
barcelona.why: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the only concert hall in Europe lit entirely by natural light during the day.
flow: Enter through the mosaic-pillared foyer.
Take the stairs to the main hall under the glass skylight.
Look at the stage's sculpted muses before leaving.

barcelona.name: Barceloneta Beach
barcelona.summary: The city beach at the end of the old fishermen's quarter, lined with a promenade, beach bars and seafood restaurants.
barcelona.expect: Busy in summer, with vendors on the sand; the water is calmer and cleaner further north at Nova Icària.
barcelona.tip: Eat paella in the old Barceloneta grid a few streets back from the sand.
barcelona.why: It turns a city break into a beach day without leaving the centre.
flow: Walk down from Port Vell along the marina.
Swim or sit on the sand.
Eat in the Barceloneta grid behind the beach.
barcelona.bestFor: A beach break in the city

paris.name: Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Élysées
paris.summary: Napoleon's triumphal arch at the top of the Champs-Élysées, with a rooftop terrace looking down twelve avenues.
paris.expect: Reach it by the underground passage, never across the roundabout; the terrace is 284 steps up.
paris.tip: Go up near sunset, then walk down the Champs-Élysées towards Concorde.
paris.why: It holds the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and frames the city's great east-west axis from the Louvre to La Défense.
flow: Take the underpass from the Champs-Élysées.
See the eternal flame at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
Climb to the roof terrace for the view.

paris.name: Catacombs of Paris
paris.summary: Tunnels of former limestone quarries lined with the bones of some six million Parisians moved from the city's cemeteries.
paris.expect: A 1.5 km one-way walk underground, 20 m down, with 131 steps down and 112 up; cool and damp all year.
paris.tip: Book a timed ticket well ahead; walk-up queues are long and tickets sell out.
paris.why: The ossuary was created in the 1780s when overflowing cemeteries became a health hazard.
flow: Descend at Place Denfert-Rochereau.
Walk the quarry galleries to the ossuary.
Exit at Rue Rémy-Dumoncel.

paris.name: Musée de l'Orangerie
paris.summary: A small museum in the Tuileries built around Monet's eight huge Water Lilies panels in two oval rooms.
paris.expect: Compact and calm compared with the Louvre or Orsay; an hour is enough.
paris.tip: Combine it with Orsay across the river on the same ticket deal.
paris.why: Monet designed the oval rooms himself so the Water Lilies would surround the viewer in natural light.
flow: Start in the two Water Lilies rooms.
Go downstairs to the Walter-Guillaume collection.
Walk out through the Tuileries Garden.

london.name: Buckingham Palace
london.summary: The monarch's London residence, seen from the gates for the Changing of the Guard or inside on a summer tour of the State Rooms.
london.expect: The guard ceremony draws big crowds; the State Rooms open only in summer, with timed tickets.
london.tip: Watch the guards along The Mall or at Wellington Barracks for a clearer view than the palace gates.
london.why: It has been the working headquarters of the British monarchy since 1837.
flow: Walk up The Mall from Trafalgar Square.
Watch the Changing of the Guard if it is running.
Cross St James's Park to Westminster.

london.name: St Paul's Cathedral
london.summary: Christopher Wren's domed cathedral, rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1666, with galleries climbing to the top of the dome.
london.expect: The ticket covers the crypt and the Whispering, Stone and Golden galleries; the top is 528 steps up.
london.tip: Climb to the Golden Gallery for one of the best views of the City, then cross the Millennium Bridge to Tate Modern.
london.why: Its dome survived the Blitz and became a symbol of London's resilience.
flow: See the nave and the dome from below.
Climb to the Whispering Gallery and on to the Golden Gallery.
Visit the crypt with Nelson and Wellington's tombs.
london.bestFor: Architecture and a view over the City

london.name: Victoria and Albert Museum
london.summary: The world's leading museum of art and design, from Raphael cartoons and Asian ceramics to fashion and jewellery.
london.expect: Free and enormous, with a calm garden café; pick a few galleries.
london.tip: Pair it with the Natural History Museum next door and look at the Cast Courts.
london.why: It holds more than two million objects spanning 5,000 years of design.
flow: Start in the Cast Courts.
See the fashion gallery and the jewellery rooms.
Rest in the John Madejski Garden.

amsterdam.name: Dam Square and the Royal Palace
amsterdam.summary: The city's central square with the 17th-century Royal Palace, built as the town hall at the height of the Dutch Golden Age.
amsterdam.expect: The palace is open most days except during royal events; the square itself is busy and noisy.
amsterdam.tip: Look up at the Citizens' Hall marble floor maps inside the palace.
amsterdam.why: It was the largest town hall in Europe when built and shows the confidence of Golden Age Amsterdam.
flow: Cross the square from the National Monument.
Tour the palace with the audio guide.
Walk on to the Nieuwe Kerk next door.
amsterdam.bestFor: Golden Age history in the centre

amsterdam.name: Begijnhof
amsterdam.summary: A quiet hidden courtyard of almshouses around a garden, home to a lay religious community from the 14th century.
amsterdam.expect: A residential courtyard: keep voices down; open in the daytime only.
amsterdam.tip: Enter by the gate off the Spui and look for Het Houten Huis, one of the two oldest wooden houses in the city.
amsterdam.why: It is one of the oldest inner courts in Amsterdam and a calm break from the centre.
flow: Enter from Spui.
Walk around the garden and the English Reformed Church.
See the wooden house at number 34.
amsterdam.bestFor: A quiet corner off the busy centre

madrid.name: Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum
madrid.summary: A private collection filling the gaps between the Prado and the Reina Sofía, from Italian primitives to Impressionists and Pop Art.
madrid.expect: Easier to see in a morning than the Prado; free on Monday afternoons for the permanent collection.
madrid.tip: Start on the top floor and work down chronologically.
madrid.why: Together with the Prado and Reina Sofía it forms Madrid's 'Golden Triangle of Art'.
flow: Take the lift to the second floor for early European art.
Work down through Dutch and Impressionist rooms.
Finish with 20th-century art on the ground floor.
madrid.bestFor: Art lovers wanting breadth in one visit

madrid.name: Temple of Debod
madrid.summary: A 2nd-century BC Egyptian temple rebuilt on a hilltop park, given to Spain for helping save Nubian monuments from the Aswan Dam.
madrid.expect: The small interior has limited entry; the park around it is free and busy at sunset.
madrid.tip: Come for sunset over the Casa de Campo, then walk down to the Royal Palace.
madrid.why: It is one of the few ancient Egyptian temples that can be seen outside Egypt.
flow: Walk up through the Parque del Oeste.
See the temple reflected in its pool.
Watch the sunset from the viewing terrace.

prague.name: Wenceslas Square
prague.summary: The long boulevard-square of the New Town, crowned by the National Museum and the statue of St Wenceslas.
prague.expect: Commercial and busy; the history matters more than the shops.
prague.tip: Look for the memorial to Jan Palach below the National Museum.
prague.why: Crowds gathered here in 1918, 1968 and 1989; it is where the Velvet Revolution was won.
flow: Start at the National Museum end.
See the St Wenceslas statue and Palach memorial.
Walk down to Můstek and on to the Old Town.
prague.bestFor: Modern Czech history in one walk

istanbul.name: İstiklal Avenue and Taksim
istanbul.summary: The 1.4 km pedestrian street from Taksim Square to Galata, with its red nostalgic tram, arcades, churches and side-street bars.
istanbul.expect: Very crowded in the evenings and at weekends.
istanbul.tip: Ride the nostalgic tram one way and walk back, ducking into Çiçek Pasajı and the side streets of Cihangir.
istanbul.why: It was the grand avenue of 19th-century Pera, lined with embassies and arcades.
flow: Start at Taksim Square.
Walk past Çiçek Pasajı and St Anthony's Church.
Finish at Galata Tower down the hill.
istanbul.bestFor: An evening walk in modern Istanbul

athens.name: Temple of Olympian Zeus
athens.summary: The colossal ruined temple to Zeus, finished by Hadrian, whose 15 surviving columns stand beside Hadrian's Arch.
athens.expect: An open site with little shade, quickly seen; included in the combined Acropolis ticket.
athens.tip: Visit after the Acropolis on the combined ticket and walk on to the Panathenaic Stadium.
athens.why: It was the largest temple in Greece, taking almost 650 years to finish.
flow: Pass through Hadrian's Arch.
Walk around the standing columns.
Continue to the Panathenaic Stadium.
